rejected.title: Embedding evidence
card: Embedding means building a short quotation into your own sentence, so your sentence still reads smoothly. Quote only the few words you need.
Example
The narrator calls the harbour "a grey mouth", which makes the water seem hungry.
Do not drop a long quotation in on its own line or leave it unexplained. Do not let the quotation do the work that your analysis should do.
After the quotation, analyse its language. Name a word or technique, such as a metaphor, and explain the effect on the reader.
rejected.remember: Quote a few words inside your sentence, then analyse the language.

a.q: Using an invented poem, which sentence embeds evidence best?
opts: The street becomes "a river of rust", implying decay
The street is shown. "A river of rust". It implies decay
The street becomes a rusty river, implying decay
The poem implies decay, as the street is a river of rust
a.why: The first option builds the poet's exact words, in quotation marks, into a smooth sentence and then names the effect. The second leaves the quotation loose as a fragment on its own. The third paraphrases and the fourth drops the quotation marks, so neither shows which words are the poet's.
a.clue: Look for the poet's marked words inside one smooth sentence.

b.q: A student quotes "the clock ticked like a warning" from an invented story. What should come next?
opts: Analysis of the simile and how it creates a sense of threat
Another quotation from a different scene about the clock
A retelling of the whole scene in which the clock appears
A statement that the quotation proves the story is good
b.why: Close reading needs analysis of the language right after the quotation, here the simile and its effect. Adding another quotation or retelling the scene does not explain how the words work.
b.clue: What must follow a quotation to show close reading?
